Connecting the places where children learn and receive care | UNICEF Digital Impact
Article
Connecting the places where children learn and receive care
UNICEF invites 96 companies to help expand internet access across all 54 African countries
UNICEF Digital Inclusion | Delivery Solutions
Giga/UNICEF-ITU
03 September 2026
A reliable internet connection can transform an ordinary day in a school. It can give a teacher access to new learning materials, help a student explore a world beyond the classroom, and link an isolated school to services and opportunities that many others take for granted. In a health facility, the same connection can help health workers find vital information and provide better care for children and families.
Yet many schools and health facilities across the world remain offline, and children in rural and low-income communities are the most excluded.
UNICEF is working with African governments and the private sector to change this. As part of a continent-wide procurement initiative, UNICEF has invited 96 companies to bid for long-term agreements to provide reliable, affordable internet connectivity to schools, health facilities and other places serving children, across all 54 African countries.
“A rising generation of more than 700 million children and young people in Africa is ready to shape the connected world, but only if they can reach it. Closing that gap is how we turn connectivity into information, opportunity and choice for every child, wherever they are born.” said Kaan Çetintürk, Chief Information Officer at UNICEF.
The invited companies include global satellite providers, pan-African telecommunications operators, national internet service providers and research and education networks. They were prequalified through a public Request for Expressions of Interest and an in-depth market analysis. Together, they can serve every country in scope, a potential universe of more than 860,000 schools and 260,000 health facilities.
The Request for Proposals, launched by UNICEF’s Supply Division and Digital Impact Division, is the competitive phase of the initiative announced earlier this year. Selected suppliers will deliver end-to-end connectivity services that meet clear standards for quality, child safeguarding and accountability.
Giga/UNICEF-ITU
“A rising generation of more than 700 million children and young people in Africa is ready to shape the connected world, but only if they can reach it. Closing that gap is how we turn connectivity into information, opportunity and choice for every child, wherever they are born.”
The tender covers three areas, so that companies of every profile can compete for what they do best:
Internet connectivity: reliable internet delivered to each facility;
On-site networks: Wi-Fi, cabling and equipment that make connectivity usable in classrooms and consultation rooms;
Solar power: clean energy for facilities without reliable electricity, because in much of the continent the connectivity gap is also an energy gap.
Every contract will include enforceable commitments on speed, uptime and repair times, along with child-appropriate online protection and cybersecurity requirements. Performance will be monitored in real time and shared through open data, building on Giga Maps, the open platform that has already mapped the location and connectivity status of more than 500,000 schools across Africa.
Once suppliers are selected, governments will be able to contract connectivity through UNICEF’s procurement services via fast, competitive bidding among the selected companies. This will help countries move from planning to connected classrooms and clinics in months rather than years, with solutions adapted to different national and local realities, from densely populated cities to remote communities.
Proposals are due by 6 November 2026, and the first agreements are expected in 2027.

The Gambia puts its health facilities on the map | UNICEF Digital Impact
Article
The Gambia puts its health facilities on the map
How connectivity and digitalization are set to transform health and education services for children in The Gambia
UNICEF Digital Inclusion
UNICEF Gambia
16 September 2026
Much of The Gambia's fibre backbone follows the River Gambia corridor. That concentration leaves the network dependent on a limited number of routes, and it increases the challenge of extending reliable and affordable connectivity in the last mile to the health facilities, schools and social service locations where public services are delivered to children across the country.
The Government of The Gambia is investing to digitally transform the essential public services that support health workers, teachers and social welfare staff in delivering better outcomes for children. To help realize the return on those investments, the Government invited the UNICEF Digital Inclusion team to collaborate on exploring how affordable and sustainable internet connectivity can help strengthen these services.
As in many other parts of the world, the price of a gigabyte in The Gambia is high. That places internet access in the country among the higher-cost environments globally, for public institutions and households alike, and it remains a major barrier to digital inclusion. This affordability gap risks deepening existing inequalities and limiting the potential of digital technologies to expand access to education, health information, public services, civic participation and economic opportunities.
Embedded video follows
UNICEF Digital Impact
In the West Coast Region, the Farato Health Centre is central to the life of the surrounding communities. Mothers come for antenatal care and childbirth, children come for routine check-ups and immunization, and community members come for treatment and other essential health services. The facility also provides digital birth registration services, making it an important access point for parents seeking to register the births of their children. It is a location where connectivity could make a life-changing difference.
"We did have an internet connection here before, but it's no longer functional. It's dormant at the moment. And it was very essential for the operation of the day-to-day activities of the facility," says Lamin Wally, a health care worker at Farato. "We're using it especially for digital birth registration that we are doing at the facility here. When we have these connections, it is going to pay dividends as well."
UNICEF Gambia
When our details are written on a paper and transferred to a computer, that will be helpful and will provide evidence. But if you are given only the paper, without transferring that data into a computer, one may step out and get drenched in the rain, and on your return to the hospital you will not have any document to present. If this information were in a computer, we would not need to come with this file,
Connectivity would also change what happens to patients such as Adama Camara, a nursing mother who relies on the clinic's services for herself and her baby.
"When our details are written on a paper and transferred to a computer, that will be helpful and will provide evidence. But if you are given only the paper, without transferring that data into a computer, one may step out and get drenched in the rain, and on your return to the hospital you will not have any document to present. If this information were in a computer, we would not need to come with this file," she says - an everyday illustration of how a single computer in a facility could change what patients experience.
Fatou Touray, a data entry clerk who handles a large volume of paperwork in her daily routine, expects digitalization to make a visible difference at her facility.
"We are going into the malaria season, and in the malaria season we used to record many patients. And each patient will come with a paper, and each of them should be recorded in the register. We have a lot of work to do, but when you have the electronic system, that will make the work easier for us," she says.
Further east in the village of Kafuta, the community's basic and secondary schools - which together serve approximately 1,165 children - stand next to the village health post. The proximity creates an opportunity for cost-effective and sustainable connectivity, yet these children have limited experience of what the internet could mean for their learning and their futures.
The appetite for digitalization runs from decision-makers to frontline workers, students, parents, children and young people, and the UNICEF Country Office in The Gambia has been working closely with the Government to meet it.
"Across health, education, protection, governance and community engagement, digital infrastructure is increasingly seen not as a luxury, but as essential to better, faster and more accountable services," says Nafisa Binte Shafique, UNICEF Representative in The Gambia, after a recent mission with President Adama Barrow and the Minister of Health, Dr Ahmadou Lamin Samateh. Nafisa underlined the need for stronger primary health infrastructure closer to communities.
Global Connectivity Map
Health facilities data of The Gambia in the Global Connectivity Map: green squares show connected facilities, and red squares, unconnected.
To accelerate that collaboration, Tanya Accone, UNICEF Digital Inclusion Senior Programme Manager, visited health facilities and schools in the country twice over the past year with her team. The Gambia is the first country to share its health facility location data with UNICEF, and the data will be available on the Global Connectivity Map from 16 September 2026.
"Children and families rely every day on health and education locations. These are the places where families seek care, where children learn and where vital support is delivered," says Accone. "Making internet connectivity more affordable and sustainable is central to the delivery of inclusive, digitally enabled services that support children throughout their lives."

How Lesotho is protecting children and their families in a digital age | UNICEF Digital Impact
Article
How Lesotho is protecting children and their families in a digital age
Testing for vulnerabilities, training staff, and even piloting new cybersecurity controls specific to children
Innocent Kafembe
UNICEF/UNI912179/Kafembe
05 December 2025
At the government office in Maseru, a team of staff surrounds a screen led by the Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Communication. Fully engaged and examining every detail, they are assessing their cybersecurity requirements ahead of a cybersecurity drill. Their aim is to safeguard the digital systems that support thousands of families relying on social services.
Lesotho’s social protection and service provision platforms hold sensitive information about children and families. If that data were ever compromised, the consequences could be devastating.
As a result, UNICEF, with support from the Luxembourg Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is assisting the government in strengthening its cyber defences. Through the Safe Child project, Lesotho is carrying out a comprehensive Cyber Readiness Assessment.
“We are proud to be working with UNICEF to embed child rights into our digital systems. This is not just about technology, it’s about equity and access.”
This involves testing for vulnerabilities, training staff, and even piloting new cybersecurity controls specific to children.
Mr Kanono Ramashamole, the Principal Secretary in the Ministry of Communication, echoes this commitment: “We are proud to be working with UNICEF to embed child rights into our digital systems. This is not just about technology, it’s about equity and access.”
One of the most innovative tools being used is the Child Rights Cyber Maturity Addendum. It helps assess how well systems protect children’s data and whether they’re prepared for digital risks that could affect young users.
UNICEF/UNI912178/Kafembe
Ma Nkhahle, a recipient of the social security grant in Lesotho, pictured at home with her children.
For families like the Nkhahles, who depend on these systems for monthly child grants, this work is invisible but vital. “I never thought about hackers,” says ‘Ma Nkhahle. “But now I know the government is protecting our information. That means a lot.”
The Cyber Readiness programme is about more than firewalls it’s about foresight. It’s about ensuring that digital threats never become real-world harm for children.”
Deepak Bhaskaran, UNICEF Representative in Lesotho, emphasizes: “Cybersecurity is a child protection issue. When we secure the systems that serve children, we’re safeguarding their futures.”
Mr Ramashamole agrees: “We are building resilience not just in our systems, but in our institutions. This work ensures that Lesotho is prepared to protect its most vulnerable citizens in a digital age.”
UNICEF’s Chief of Social Policy adds: “The Cyber Readiness programme is about more than firewalls it’s about foresight. It’s about ensuring that digital threats never become real-world harm for children.”
By investing in cybersecurity today, Lesotho is building digital resilience for tomorrow and ensuring the right to digital protection for all children.
UNICEF/UNI912164/Kafembe

pages.title: Indigenous adolescents use technology to preserve healing through nature
pages.text:
Indigenous adolescents use technology to preserve healing through nature | UNICEF Digital Impact
Article
Indigenous adolescents use technology to preserve healing through nature
Students from the Antônio Saymã Indigenous State School, in Uiramutã, Brazil, transform elders’ knowledge into videos, bringing together Indigenous tradition and digital innovation
UNICEF
©UNICEF/BRZ/Katarine Almeida
12 August 2026
UNICEF/BRZ/Katarine Almeida
“Traditional medicine has always been part of my life. When I have cramps, I drink chamomile tea , I learned about its benefits from my mother,” says 15-year-old Ester Lima. Alongside classmates Wendel Silva and Ryane Leite, both 15 years old, Ester took part in a medicinal garden project at the Antônio Saymã Indigenous State School. Created to serve the community and revive the use of plants as a source of healing, the project faced a challenge after its conclusion: how to encourage the ongoing care and use of medicinal herbs in a context where ancestral knowledge was being lost? The answer began to take shape with the arrival of the Territórios Conectados (Connected Territories) project, a UNICEF initiative.
With the connectivity provided by the project, the school gained internet access as well as the necessary support to develop innovative pedagogical practices and strengthen learning and digital skills across the entire school community. Motivated by this new scenario, adolescents joined teachers Lidiane Ribeiro and Nazione da Silva to use technology as a tool to document, value and preserve traditional knowledge and community memories. From this collaboration emerged the initiative “Medicinal Garden: Preserving Macuxi Indigenous Knowledge”, a series of videos dedicated to passing ancestral knowledge on to present and future generations.
To make this possible, students and teachers received training in communication and activism, in addition to learning how to use new technologies and harness their potential for education. After acquiring the necessary foundational skills, it was time to speak directly with the sources of all this knowledge: the grandfathers and grandmothers , as the community elders are affectionately called.
The adolescents closely followed each elder’s accounts, recording stories on tablets and through educational videos. “For me, being part of a project that values what I inherited from my mother and allows me to share this learning beyond the community is very meaningful,” explains Wendel Silva. His mother, a nurse in the region, was one of those responsible for strengthening local knowledge about the use of medicinal herbs.
UNICEF/BRZ/Katarine Almeida
“The project brought technology to our school and strengthened knowledge and learning, enabling us to preserve our Macuxi Indigenous knowledge , our medicinal garden,”
UNICEF/BRZ/Katarine Almeida
The adolescents visited elders’ homes and learned about preservation, plants and remedies. Everything was carefully documented on the tablets and mobile phones that accompanied them throughout the journey.
All traditional knowledge that was once passed down orally between generations has gained a new form of expression and is now also shared on social media. “Everything is very new for us , using tablets, video editing software, social media, doing research. I found it all very interesting,” says Ryane Leite.
“The project brought technology to our school and strengthened knowledge and learning, enabling us to preserve our Macuxi Indigenous knowledge , our medicinal garden,” highlights teacher Nazione da Silva.
About the Territórios Conectados (Connected Territories) initiative
UNICEF works in Brazil to strengthen the right of every girl and boy to attend school and learn. More than ever, it recognizes that the full development of children and adolescents requires access to connectivity and to a comprehensive education that considers and integrates new digital information and communication technologies (ICTs).
Since 2021, through the Territórios Conectados (Connected Territories) project, UNICEF has partnered with civil society organizations to develop and document experiences in schools across different regions of Brazil. The initiative is part of UNICEF’s global Learning Passport programme, which serves as a technical and digital accelerator for several other projects focused on promoting continuous access to digital education.
In 2025, the project worked with 105 schools in the states of Amazonas, Roraima, Ceará, Pernambuco, Maranhão and Rio Grande do Norte. Of these, 47 are Indigenous schools, 28 are quilombola schools, 6 are in settlement areas, and 24 are in small municipalities. In Roraima alone, 34 Indigenous state schools were connected and received digital devices, more than 100 educators were trained, and 5,112 students were reached by the project’s strategies, which include training in digital literacy, communication and youth activism.
In the state, the project is implemented by Casa da Árvore, with institutional support from the State Secretariat of Education and Sports of Roraima (SEED), the State Center for the Training of Education Professionals of Roraima (CEFORR), the Organization of Indigenous Teachers of Roraima (OPIRR) and the Association of Indigenous Peoples of the São Marcos Indigenous Land (APITSM).
For this initiative, UNICEF is supported through a global partnership with F1 and Adyen.
UNICEF does not endorse any brand, service or product.

pages.text:
Lesotho’s Digital Public Infrastructure drive | UNICEF Digital Impact

Lesotho’s Digital Public Infrastructure drive | UNICEF Digital Impact
Article
Lesotho’s Digital Public Infrastructure drive
Building better for every child
Innocent Kafembe
UNICEF/UNI912170/Kafembe
11 December 2025
Nestled among Lesotho’s rolling highlands, the Matokele family’s village in Mafeteng District features stone rondavels, communal wells, and winding dirt paths where children play freely, herd cattle and sheep during the day, and families gather around evening fires.
Life here is deeply rooted in tradition but increasingly shaped by digital systems that provide essential social protection, including child grants, food support, and health services. As these services transition online, the risks also increase; personal data from families in remote areas is now stored on national platforms.
Without strong safeguards, this data could be exposed or misused, endangering not only privacy but also access to essential support those communities rely on. In areas where connectivity is limited and digital literacy is low, protecting children’s rights means making sure that technology benefits rather than harms.
When Matokele Ranteme receives a message from the government’s social assistance portal on her grandchild’s support status, she doesn’t think about technology or data. She thinks about food on the table, school fees paid on time, and the dignity of being seen by the system.
“We’re not just building technology, we’re building trust. That starts with asking: who might be left out? Who might be harmed?”
But behind that simple login is a quiet transformation. Lesotho is redesigning its digital public systems, beginning with those that impact children. With support from UNICEF and the Co-Develop Fund, the country is integrating child rights into the core of its digital infrastructure. The Lesotho National Information System for Social Assistance (NISSA) is a social registry where household information is stored, and households are categorized based on their vulnerability level.
The NISSA contains information on over ninety percent of all households in Lesotho. The purpose of this household information system is to help identify families in need of government support through social protection.
That means ensuring systems like NISSA are not only efficient but also fair, inclusive, and safe from the outset.
“We’re not just building technology,” says Bob Muchabaiwa, UNICEF Lesotho’s Chief of Social Policy. “We’re building trust. That starts with asking: who might be left out? Who might be harmed?”
The new safeguards help prevent children from being excluded due to lack of documentation, disability, or where they live. They also ensure that children’s personal data is protected from misuse. These changes are guided by the Universal DPI Safeguards Framework, which helps governments design systems that work for everyone, especially the most vulnerable.
UNICEF/UNI912170/Kafembe
Mr Kanono Ramashamole. The Principal Secretary in the Lesotho Ministry of Information, Communication, Science, Technology and Innovation
For Matokele, this means she no longer has to spend hours traveling to a government office to receive her grandchildren’s payments. “I can do it from my phone now,” she says. “And I know it’s safe.”
Her granddaughter Katleho is excited to be attending school now. “What I like the most about school is Science, Math, and English. When I grow up, I want to be a doctor,” she says with a smile.
“We’re focusing on a holistic approach,” says Mr Kanono Ramashande, the Principal Secretary in the Ministry of Communication. “UNICEF is one of our key partners, especially when it comes to DPI. As the ministry, we are not shy to admit that DPI was introduced to us by UNICEF. Even though we are now taking it further by conducting pilots, we are also working closely with UNICEF on DPI safeguards. We will therefore collaborate with them to establish our own local DPI safeguards framework,” he adds.
UNICEF’s Chief of Social Policy concludes: “The DPI Safeguards programme is a blueprint for ethical digital development. It’s about building systems that don’t just deliver services but deliver fairness, dignity, and protection.”
“Digital transformation must be inclusive from the start. These safeguards ensure that no child is left behind, and that families can access services with confidence and dignity.”
UNICEF/UNI912167/Kafembe
Deepak Bhaskaran, UNICEF Representative in Lesotho
Deepak Bhaskaran, UNICEF Representative in Lesotho, adds: “Digital transformation must be inclusive from the start. These safeguards ensure that no child is left behind, and that families can access services with confidence and dignity.”
Lesotho’s approach is already inspiring other countries in the region. By putting children at the centre of digital design, it’s proving that technology can be a bridge, not a barrier to opportunity.

Putting children at the centre of independent AI evaluation | UNICEF Digital Impact
Article
Putting children at the centre of independent AI evaluation
At UNGA, UNICEF joined partners to advance a global AI evaluation ecosystem that puts children first.
UNICEF
UNICEF/UNI960921/Mkhize
08 October 2026
Tatiana Valeria/ArtVesta Studio
Participants attending the event "Interoperable Practice, Policy and Investment: Building an International and Independent AI Evaluation Ecosystem"
On 23 September 2026, UNICEF co-hosted a UN General Assembly (UNGA) side event in New York with Humane Intelligence and the UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR), bringing together over 100 policymakers, researchers, civil society, funders and technology leaders to explore a pressing question: how can we build an independent AI evaluation ecosystem that serves the public interest?
The event, Interoperable Practice, Policy and Investment: Building an International and Independent AI Evaluation Ecosystem, also marked the launch of the Independent AI Evaluation Foundation (IAEF).
For UNICEF, the central message was clear: children must not be treated as an afterthought in the development and evaluation of AI.
Tatiana Valeria/ArtVesta Studio
Lily Caprani, UNICEF's Chief of Global Advocacy, delivers opening remarks at the event.
Opening the event, Lily Caprani, UNICEF's Chief of Global Advocacy, emphasized that evaluating AI for children must go beyond preventing the most serious harms. It should also consider whether AI supports children's learning, development, and ability to exercise their rights. “We don’t just want to prevent the worst from happening. We want to make sure that children who are using AI in their daily lives are actually learning and flourishing.”
AI systems are increasingly being used by children, yet most evaluation approaches were not designed with children in mind. In a panel discussion, UNICEF Chief AI, Henrietta Ridley, highlighted several challenges in building AI evaluations for children.
First, children do not experience AI in the same way. Their needs and experiences can vary depending on their age, language, culture, and circumstances. Any AI evaluation must account for these differences.
Second, some risks of AI may only emerge over time. This means evaluations should look not only at individual interactions, but also at how children engage with AI over repeated use.
Third, safety alone is not enough. It is important to check whether AI avoids harmful responses, but we also need to understand whether it supports children's dignity, development, and well-being.
Tatiana Valeria/ArtVesta Studio
Henrietta Ridley, Chief AI, UNICEF (centre), highlights the importance of AI benchmarking for children during a panel discussion.
"Please stop treating children as an edge case, we have to make sure that children are involved in the benchmarking and in the evaluations of these systems that they are using every day."
Building momentum for independent AI evaluation for children
The discussion concluded with calls for governments, technology companies, funders and evaluation experts to strengthen collaboration and invest in the institutions, practices and standards needed for independent AI evaluation.
The event builds on growing international momentum to ensure children's rights are protected in the digital world, including the recently launched Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI , of which UNICEF is a co-founder.
UNICEF will continue working with partners to ensure children's voices, experiences and rights are part of how AI is evaluated, governed and used.

Have you ever heard of the swarming of tanajuras or the legends of the Canaimé? If these sound mysterious to you, you can learn more about them on the Instagram profile @cailainterativo . The account exists thanks to the leadership of adolescents from the Água Fria community, located in the Raposa Serra do Sol Indigenous Land, in Uiramutã, Roraima, Brazil , leadership made possible by access to connectivity promoted through the Territórios Conectados (Connected Territories) project, an initiative of UNICEF. Through this experience, students from the São Sebastião do Cailã Indigenous State School began using the internet to show the world the cultural richness and daily life of those who live in one of the most fascinating regions of the state.
Embedded video follows
After living in the community for two years, teacher Ranylson Leocádio dreamed of sharing with the world everything he witnessed there. It was in this context that he met the adolescents Edjane Barbosa, Elano Dias, Leuziane Clementino and Yara Filgueiras. Through Territórios Conectados (Connected Territories), the group turned plans into action and imagination into reality. “When I arrived in Água Fria, I found a place full of peculiarities , ways of life, tales, legends, stories,” the teacher explains. Through digital literacy training and the use of technologies to strengthen education offered by the project, the adolescents began creating content portraying everyday life in the community, such as the preparation of genipap dye, the production of cassava flour, and the meaning of body paintings used in festivities. Over time, however, they went further: they adopted artificial intelligence-based tools to create scripts and recreate images of legends told by elders, transforming this knowledge into content for social media.
UNICEF/BRZ/Katarine Almeida
“When I arrived in Água Fria, I found a place full of peculiarities , ways of life, tales, legends, stories,”
As part of the digital literacy training and the use of technologies to boost education, the adolescents started producing content that shows daily community life, including the making of genipap dye, cassava flour production, and the significance of body paintings used during celebrations. Soon, they went beyond that and began using artificial intelligence-based tools to develop scripts and recreate images of legends shared by elders, turning these stories into content for the project’s social media platforms.
The search for new content led the adolescents to engage in dialogue with community elders, local researchers and anyone who could help them share fragments of the territory’s vast culture and history with the world. Throughout the project, they also began visiting little-known places, such as sites with drawings engraved on stones, whose origins even the elders cannot explain.
“It is hard to open social media and not find faces and stories that represent me. We really want to show our Macuxi and Ingarikó identity to the world,” says Yara Filgueiras, the adolescent influencer who appears in the Cailã Interativo videos. According to her, students are overcoming their shyness, and now that Cailã Interativo has grown, they are even happier to take part.
About the Territórios Conectados (Connected Territories) initiative
UNICEF works in Brazil to strengthen every girl’s and every boy’s right to be in school and learning. More than ever, it recognizes that the full development of children and adolescents requires access to connectivity and to a comprehensive education that considers and integrates new digital information and communication technologies (ICTs). Since 2021, through the Territórios Conectados (Connected Territories) project, UNICEF has partnered with civil society organizations to develop and document experiences in schools across different regions of Brazil.
The initiative is part of UNICEF’s global Learning Passport programme, which serves as a technical and digital accelerator for several other projects focused on promoting continuous access to digital education.
In 2025, the project worked with 105 schools in the states of Amazonas, Roraima, Ceará, Pernambuco, Maranhão and Rio Grande do Norte. Of these, 47 are Indigenous schools, 28 are quilombola schools, 6 are in settlement areas, and 24 are in small municipalities. In Roraima alone, 34 Indigenous state schools were connected and received digital devices, more than 100 educators were trained, and 5,112 students were reached by the project’s strategies, which include training in digital literacy, communication and youth activism.
In the state, the project is implemented by Casa da Árvore, with institutional support from the State Secretariat of Education and Sports of Roraima (SEED), the State Center for the Training of Education Professionals of Roraima (CEFORR), the Organization of Indigenous Teachers of Roraima (OPIRR) and the Association of Indigenous Peoples of the São Marcos Indigenous Land (APITSM).
For this initiative, UNICEF is supported through a global partnership with F1 and Adyen.

pages.title: When a phone becomes a lifeline for families in emergencies
pages.text:
When a phone becomes a lifeline for families in emergencies | UNICEF Digital Impact
Article
When a phone becomes a lifeline for families in emergencies
Innovation doesn’t always mean new technology. Sometimes, it’s about finding new ways to use what’s already in place: a reliable database, a phone, and the trust built with communities.
UNICEF
UNICEF
10 June 2025
What stays behind after a cash transfer programme using mobile phone or ‘mobile money’ ends? Income generating activities, better meals on the table, children back in school, long lasting changes… and often, a simple mobile phone.
In Minova, a town nestled between Lake Kivu and the mountains of South Kivu in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, that phone - initially provided to support a previous cash assistance project - became a lifeline for thousands of families in January 2025 as violence flared across the region.
The town was among the first to feel the impact of the escalating violence early 2025. At that time, the 300,000 displaced people who had sought safety in Minova were pushed into even deeper hardship. Families displaced from other conflict areas who were living in camps, churches or even schools were often left with nothing following the dismantling of displacement sites and new mass displacement.
For humanitarian actors, losing access to the area meant operating with limited visibility. Without being able to reach Minova, UNICEF and its partners had to find new ways to quickly understand and respond to families’ needs.
"We were facing an exceptional crisis and had to change how we worked," explains UNICEF Emergency Specialist Jean Wilner Bassette. “We needed a way to understand the situation of families in Minova without putting anyone at risk.”
Then came an idea, one that changed everything.
In December 2023, more than 14,000 families had received mobile phones as part of an integrated programme to prevent gender-based violence and other protection risks that included a cash assistance component. When this programme started, the first activity after identifying participants was the distribution of phones with activated mobile money accounts.
Those phones, if still in use, could be the key.
Through the RapidPro platform, an interactive SMS application, UNICEF sent out a survey to all the families. Within 24 hours, hundreds had responded. By the end of the week, more than 9,000 families had shared information about where they were, how they were doing, and what they needed. They also confirmed that their mobile money accounts were still active and, most critically, that there were functioning cash points that they could safely access.
UNICEF
Espérance Shukuru holds her daughter Jordanna in Goma, North Kivu, DR Congo, on 9 April 2025. Through her phone, she receives support as part of a humanitarian cash transfer programme.
Espérance Shukuru , a mother of three, has been displaced for most of her life. She was just eight years old the first time she had to flee her home. “When the latest crisis broke out, we were asked to leave the displacement sites,” she explains. Fortunately, she still had her phone and was able to respond to UNICEF’s survey.
It was a game-changer as the responses provided a real-time snapshot of the situation. Because family data was already in UNICEF’s Humanitarian cash Operations and Programme Ecosystem (HOPE) platform, the team could launch one of the first large-scale humanitarian interventions in eastern DRC and the first cash intervention in Minova during the current crisis.
These bulk transfers were also the first time for UNICEF to use its global contract with Western Union to deliver money via ‘mobile’ wallets at scale. This allowed cash teams to issue payments almost immediately after phone numbers and mobile money accounts were verified as functional.
“Those who answered first were the first to receive support,” says Programme Officer Muhindo Mbonzo. “We didn’t need to send teams into insecure zones to register people or assess needs.”
Since the first cash transfers started on 7 March, the programme reached more than of 6,000 families, improving the living conditions of tens of thousands of people . In coming weeks, UNICEF aims to reach other families not included in the first round of support.
UNICEF
Gisèle Byamungu holds two loincloths she sells at a market in Goma, North Kivu, DR Congo, on 9 April 2025. Through her phone, she receives support as part of a humanitarian cash transfer programme.
Gisèle Byamungu and her six children arrived in Goma a few weeks ago. “Business was going well in Minova until the new crisis hit,” she recalls. “With what little money I had left, I paid for transport to get my whole family to Goma.” When she received the cash transfer from UNICEF, her priority was getting her children back into school. She also bought a few pieces of fabric, which she now sells at the local market. “I’m proud to be able to provide for my family,” she says.
Mobile cash assistance offers speed, dignity, and choice. It lets families decide what their children need most. In places with poor network coverage or limited access to cash points, UNICEF will work with partners to set up mobile cash counters for a 'cash-in-hand' distribution.
This wasn’t just about fast delivery; it was about reaching families at a critical time. And maybe the biggest lesson of all? Innovation doesn’t always mean new technology. Sometimes, it’s about finding new ways to use what’s already in place: a reliable database, a phone, and the trust built with communities.

UNICEF AI Strategy 2025-2030: AI for every child
Responsible AI to accelerate results for children and protect their rights
UNICEF
Artificial Intelligence is already reshaping how societies learn, communicate, govern and deliver services. For children, AI presents enormous opportunities, but it also raises serious concerns around privacy, safety, discrimination and exclusion.
To address both the opportunities and risks, UNICEF’s AI Strategy 2025-2030: AI for every child is a roadmap designed to ensure AI works in the best interests of children everywhere.
The strategy positions AI not simply as a technological tool, but as an accelerator for results for children while safeguarding their rights.
UNICEF AI strategy main pillars
Al for programme impact
Deliver quality, effective programme impact at scale for children and communities.
Al for operational efficiency and effectiveness
Improve readiness, productivity and business process efficiency across UNICEF.
Child rights advocacy on Al
Ensure children’s rights, voices and safety shape Al governance at every level.
Six core capabilities areas
To turn ambition into action, UNICEF has identified six core capabilities required to deliver sustainable and scalable AI implementation:
1 Strategy and value realization Focus Al on measurable benefits for children.
2 Data and AI core Trusted data, platforms and infrastructure.
3 AI risk management Guardrails, guidance and tools for responsible use.
4 People and adoption Skills, culture and new ways of working.
5 Partnerships Work with public, private, civil society and UN partners
6 Advocacy and foresight Shape the future Al agenda for child rights.
The UNICEF AI Hub
The UNICEF AI Hub links country, regional and HQ teams through seven thematic AI circles.
Responsible Al principles
UNICEF’s AI strategy adopts the “ Principles for the Ethical Use of AI in the UN system ” to establish strong responsible AI guardrails. The strategy is guided by ten key principles:
Define purpose, necessity and proportionality
Do no harm
Safety and security
Fairness and non-discrimination
Sustainability
Right to privacy, data protection and data governance
Human autonomy and oversight
Transparency and explainability
Responsibility and accountability
Inclusion and participation
These safeguards aim to build trust while reducing the risks associated with AI deployment.
Our AI vision for 2030
By 2030, UNICEF envisions becoming an AI-mature organization with:
Trusted digital foundations
Clear governance frameworks
Skilled and AI-ready teams
Strong global partnerships
A leading voice for child-centred AI

Vulnerabilities requiring physical access to a user's device
Publicly available files with no sensitive information
Missing best practices in SSL/TLS configuration
Please note that UNICEF reserves the right to accept or reject any security vulnerability disclosure report at its discretion.
To report vulnerabilities affecting other UN entities, please refer to the UN Information Security Hall of Fame .
UNICEF’s Responsible Disclosure Policy
UNICEF is committed to protecting children worldwide, and that commitment extends to securing our digital assets to strengthen the protection of our Information and Communications Technology infrastructure, UNICEF actively encourages the global security community to partner with us by responsibly disclosing vulnerabilities in our publicly accessible information systems.
We deeply value the expertise and contributions of security researchers in identifying potential security issues. This collaborative approach allows us to continuously improve our security posture and better safeguard our mission of helping children around the world.
This site provides guidelines for security researchers conducting vulnerability research and reporting, while also recognizing those who have made valuable contributions to our security efforts. Together, we can ensure that UNICEF's digital resources remain secure, allowing us to focus on what matters most , improving the lives of children everywhere.
Safe harbor
We follow safe harbor principles for security researchers who:
Make good faith efforts to avoid privacy violations, destruction of data, and interruption or degradation of our services. This includes limiting access to sensitive data - if researchers discover a vulnerability allowing access to sensitive data, they may access a minimal amount necessary to verify findings, but must not download complete datasets
Only interact with accounts they own or with explicit permission of the account holder
Do not exploit a security issue they discover for any reason beyond verification
Report vulnerabilities directly to us as soon as possible after its discovery
Keep information about any vulnerabilities confidential until they have been resolved
As long as you comply with this policy:
We will not initiate legal action related to your research
We will work with you to understand and resolve the issue quickly
We will recognize your contribution if requested
Recognition
Upon security researchers’ request, we can acknowledge contributions in our hall of fame, which includes:
Researcher's name or handle (as preferred)
Description of the vulnerability (with appropriate redactions)
Date of report and resolution
Reporting process
How to submit a report
Please submit vulnerability reports via email to [email protected] with the subject line "Vulnerability Report: [Brief Description]".
Your report should include:
Clear description of the vulnerability
Steps to reproduce and including screenshots and any tools used
Potential impact of the vulnerability
Time frame during which the testing took place
Any supporting materials (proof of concept code, etc.)
Subject to necessary verification, if the vulnerability report complies with our Responsible Vulnerability Disclosure Policy, please indicate whether you would like to be acknowledged in UNICEF’s Information Security Hall of Fame.
What to expect
Acknowledgment: Receipt of your report will be acknowledged within 3 business days.
Evaluation: The report will be assessed, and the team may request additional information.
Resolution: Verified vulnerabilities will be remediated, keeping you informed of our progress (typically within 90 days).
Recognition: The timing and details of public acknowledgement will be coordinated with security researchers.
We deeply value the expertise and contributions of security researchers in identifying potential security issues
Contact
For questions regarding this policy, please contact us at [email protected] .

What we do
Digital and technology for development
The adoption and role of digital and technology in our lives has increased rapidly in recent years, affecting all parts of society, including relationships, work and public service delivery. Digital technology can help reach children and families with information and services faster and more effectively, create data and new insights into development challenges and connect children to social and economic opportunities. Today’s children and youth are more digitally skilled and connected than any other generation, and youth play a critical role in utilizing digital technology to build a more sustainable future.
At the same time, digital divides between and within countries can exacerbate inequalities and leave children behind. For example,globally, only 33 per cent of children and young people have internet access at home.This requires us actively address the inequalities in children’s lives that lead to disparate experiences in seizing digital opportunities and avoiding digital risks.
UNICEF’s work on digital and technology for development is focused on unlocking the potential of digital transformation for child rights. Specifically, we focus on:
Strengthening foundational digital systems that underpin service delivery for child rights, for example in health and education.
Identifying and applying digital, technology and data solutions to deliver services and information to children more quickly and more effectively.
Advancing digital inclusion to ensure all children benefit from digital opportunities , for example through our work on connectivity, digital skills building and more.
Capacity building and training for the use of digital systems, for example for frontline workers.

Home
What we do
Digital education
UNICEF is on the ground in over 190 countries and territories, working across borders and barriers to reach children with the learning opportunities they need to succeed. Non-political and impartial, we're never neutral when it comes to protecting a child's right to education . With over 200 colleagues working across sectors on digital education, UNICEF has the expertise needed to ensure quality learning reaches every child.
But we cannot do it alone. We team up with communities, governments and businesses to:
1. Make digital learning equitable and safe
We work with governments to make digital learning platforms and solutions run effectively offline or with limited connectivity, function on low-cost devices, are accessible and inclusive for children with disabilities, and translate into local languages and cultural contexts. Our solutions also adhere to global best practices for online safety and data protection.
2. Improve the quality of digital learning
We use evidence to design and implement digital learning programmes that are flexible and personalized, adapting to each learner's level. Our focus is on strengthening literacy and numeracy, plus digital skills, so children build a foundation for lifelong learning.
3. Integrate digital learning across settings
We build the capacity of teachers and administrators to apply digital pedagogies and technologies, and help caregivers and communities support high-tech and low-tech digital learning. We ensure digital learning reaches children in emergencies and humanitarian contexts.

Digitally enabled health systems drive results for children.
Page
Home
What we do
Digital health
UNICEF envisions a world where the health and well-being of every child is improved through digitally enabled health systems. We work with governments, donors and partners to improve the planning and implementation of digital health systems to improve primary health care.
In many places, especially low-income countries and humanitarian settings, health sector digitalization is not systematically invested in. This can result in weakened and siloed systems, create new risks to child wellbeing and increase burdens on frontline health workers. In these instances, the children most in need are often left behind.
The digital transformation (DX) of healthcare systems can revolutionize patient care and healthcare outcomes. Key to this transformation are improved capacity of healthcare workers, standards-based technologies, and data-driven decision-making.
This comprehensive approach can directly enhance efficiency, accuracy and accessibility of health services, while also facilitating better communication and coordination among healthcare professionals.
Harnessing the power of data analytics, geospatial information and artificial intelligence can lead to more personalized treatments, reduced human error, early disease detection, and proactive interventions. This can ultimately improve the quality-of-care, patient outcomes and efficiency of the healthcare staff. It can also lead to more equitable coverage and lower overall costs.
Timely, high-quality data can also expose inequities in health outcomes and help decision makers identify children’s unmet needs. This information can be used to determine how and where to invest in health facilities, staff, vaccines and other supplies, which is particularly crucial when responding to emergencies like disease outbreaks.

What we do
Digital transformation
Digital transformation has many guises. It’s a way of modifying existing operations. It’s the means of creating new ways of working. It’s a continuum rather than simply an end goal.
For UNICEF, digital transformation isn’t just about what we do. It’s also about how we do it. From how we run our organization to how we support our teams. Because our approach to digital transformation also must be driven by meeting the needs of rights holders, it covers everything from education to health and child protection to communications.
One of the core pillars of the UNICEF Strategic Plan, 2022-2025 is our Digital Transformation Change Strategy, which sets out a clear programme of work for UNICEF under four Focus Areas:
Management Efficiency and Effectiveness
Partnerships, Communication and Resource Mobilization
Digital in Programmes and Programme Effectiveness
Normative and Policy
In essence, UNICEF's digital transformation is a holistic endeavor that permeates every aspect of our work, ensuring we are more efficient, effective, and responsive to the needs of children and their communities. By embracing this change, we are better equipped to fulfill our mission and drive impactful, sustainable development worldwide for every child.

Girls and technology
Digital technology is essential to children’s and young people’s development, providing access to education, health information, creative expression, peer connection, and career opportunities.
However, a gender digital divide exists, with girls having less access to and use of technology than boys, limiting their benefits. Digital products and services are often designed for a "default" user, typically male, overlooking girls' digital realities like connectivity, device access, and digital literacy. Not designing with and for girls, including girls with disabilities, means that female user numbers are often very low, and girls risk being left behind in the digital world.
Girls and Tech harnesses tech for gender equality, to ensure digital for, with, and by girls.
Areas of focus include the gender digital divide for girls, digital literacy and gender, digital solutions for and with girls, AI and gender, digital inclusion for girls with disabilities, privacy and data protection and online safety.

Technology for emergencies
The 'Technology for Emergencies' (T4E) team at UNICEF uses digital tools to help prepare for and respond to emergencies.
We work closely with UNICEF's Emergency Operations (EMOPS) and other technology partners to create and improve digital solutions that aid children during crises. Our work includes preparing UNICEF country offices, governments, and local partners for emergencies by providing digital tools, planning, training, and support. The team aims to make emergency responses more efficient and effective through digital technology.

Who we are
Digital technology is an unstoppable force that is shaping modern life everywhere, including children’s lives.
Home
Who we are
The world is changing faster than ever before, and so too are the challenges facing its most vulnerable people. As conflict and displacement, disasters and climate change, urbanization and disease outbreaks grow increasingly complex and interrelated, new strategies and approaches to humanitarian response and development assistance are greatly needed. At the same time, rapid advancements in digital technology, for example in generative AI, are creating new opportunities - and risks - for children. Digital divides are deepening and further excluding the most vulnerable children.
UNICEF is actively involved in leveraging digital technology to advance our mission of promoting the well-being of children around the world. UNICEF recognizes the transformative potential of digital technology in improving children's lives and is committed to using it to promote child rights everywhere. We want to make sure new technologies are inclusive and address the needs of children, women, minorities and special needs persons so all can be empowered by technology.
On this site, we provide resources and guidance around digital child rights and safety online, as well as information and updates about programmes and work we do with our partners. For the past 8 decades, we have been innovating for children and believe that new approaches, partnerships, and technologies that support the realization of children’s rights are critical to improving their lives.
